newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO's Solana to face hard bargaining in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana to face hard bargaining in Moscow.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana faces his toughest talks yet on a NATO-Russia accord when he meets Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Tuesday, diplomats say.

The latest round of talks on a post-Cold War security deal, seen as critical if the alliance's plans to expand eastwards are to proceed smoothly, follow a new hardline stand by Moscow seeking strict limits on what any new alliance members can do.

"Solana is going to have to be very tough, we (NATO) have made a generous offer which meets many Russian concerns. Whether Moscow takes it or not, enlargement is going ahead anyway," said one senior Western diplomat.
But he and other western officials said they were still optimistic a deal with Russia could be struck before a July summit in Madrid to name new members.

"We see this as a last effort to split the alliance and therefore as more tactical than substantive. Our belief is that if we keep to this line, the Russians will see they have got as much as they are going to get," the diplomat added.

Last week in Paris, Primakov said Russia hoped to sign a new partnership document with NATO in the French capital on May 27, but dismayed western governments by presenting tough demands as a condition of Russia's signature.
"It was depressingly hardline, a blast of cold air, going back on many of the things we thought we had sorted out -- particularly on military infrastructure," said one NATO military source.

Western diplomats say Primakov's latest note sought to rule out any improvement of military installations and even limit upgrades in communications facilities of prospective new members such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

NATO, set to issue formal membership invitations in July, insists it has no intention of placing nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the territory of any of the newcomers. But nor will it allow the creation of a second-class membership.

NATO officials say Russia is now looking for specific guarantees no equipment or troops would ever be transferred between old and new members, effectively ruling out any future reinforcement if those states were ever threatened.

In addition to the alliance's commitment not to deploy nuclear weapons in new member states, Russia now wants a commitment NATO will never build or upgrade facilities to take such weapons at a later date.
"It is totally unacceptable, and goes back on much of what was agreed at Helsinki," said one diplomat.

At last month's summit in Helsinki, President Bill Clinton appeared to have convinced President Boris Yeltsin the alliance's plans posed no threat to Russia and the document on offer would meet all of Moscow's security concerns.

Primakov has also told NATO governments that Moscow would like details of combat troop levels in the new members and the number of military exercises planned to take place each year with other alliance armies.

Yeltsin is due to visit Germany on Wednesday and western diplomats are hopeful that if he receives the same message as that delivered by Solana, the Russians will fall into line and bring the negotiations back on track.
"There is simply too much for them to lose," said one analyst.

Yeltsin has been invited to the Group of Seven summit of industrialised states in Denver in June, and for the first time will participate in all sessions except one breakfast of G-7 heads of state and government.
For the first time, Moscow has been involved in all the preparations for the summit -- long a demand of Yeltsin, who wanted to see Russia's status fully reflected in such a forum.
"It is inconceivable that Yeltsin would come if there was no deal on a NATO-Russia pact, the atmospherics would just be too bad," added the analyst.
